title: The Strength of Staying Put: When a Hold Counts as Training
subtitle: Isometric exercises can build strength without visible movement. Their value depends on the position you train, the way you measure progress and what else your program asks your body to do.
imageAlt: One person demonstrates a controlled wall sit while a friend watches attentively nearby.
imageConcept: A couple or pair of friends in a bright, lived-in room: one person performs a comfortable wall sit with an upright torso and relaxed face while the other observes from a respectful distance, not coaching or competing. The scene feels thoughtful and ordinary, with no gym theatrics or visible strain.
body:
In an isometric contraction, a muscle produces force without an obvious change in joint position. Holding a squat partway down, pausing in a push-up position or pressing your hands together are familiar examples. The muscle is active, but you are not repeatedly lowering and lifting through a range of motion. The word “static” describes the visible movement, not the effort: a hold can be demanding even when the body appears still.

That distinction makes isometrics easy to fit into a range of settings. You may have little equipment, limited room or a reason to practise force in one particular position. But a wall sit is not a secret shortcut, and being motionless does not automatically make an exercise easier, safer or more complete. The useful question is what capacity the hold is meant to develop.
A hold trains a particular task

Strength is not one single quality that transfers perfectly to every action. The angle of a joint, the direction of force and whether the task involves movement can all affect what you practise. A person who gets better at holding a split squat at one depth has specifically practised producing force in that position. That progress matters, but it does not by itself show how much their strength has changed elsewhere in the squat, on stairs or in a different athletic task.

Research supports a careful view of transfer. A systematic review of dynamic resistance training found a moderate task-specific effect for dynamic strength, with smaller transfer to isometric strength that had not been trained. That review examined transfer from dynamic training to isometric testing; it does not prove that isometric training transfers in the reverse direction. It does, however, underline why a result should be interpreted in terms of the task used to train and test it [2].
What the strength evidence says—and doesn’t

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis compared isometric and dynamic resistance training across 32 studies involving 621 healthy adults aged 18 to 45. The authors reported that isometric training improved measured isometric strength compared with controls and dynamic training. For isokinetic strength—strength measured while a joint moves at a controlled speed—gains were similar between the two training modes [1].

Those findings support using holds to develop strength, especially when the goal or assessment involves producing force without movement. They do not establish that holds are best for every person, muscle group or outcome. The participants were healthy adults in a defined age range, and the conclusions concern specific strength measures. They should not be stretched into claims about injury treatment, blood pressure or guaranteed improvements in everyday movement.

That boundary matters because research on a different outcome can get pulled into the conversation. A large analysis of exercise and resting blood pressure studied blood-pressure changes, not whether isometric training is a complete strength program. Evidence about one outcome cannot stand in for evidence about another.
Where holds can fit into training

Think of an isometric as one tool in a broader resistance-training menu. It can be useful when you want to practise force in a specific position, add a simple challenge without equipment, or make a movement feel more controlled before doing it dynamically. For example, a person learning a bodyweight squat might briefly pause at a comfortable depth, then continue moving through repetitions as well. Someone with a sturdy counter could press their palms into it for a short, steady effort, while a training plan might use a paused position within a larger session.

The American College of Sports Medicine’s 2026 resistance-training update emphasizes consistent resistance exercise and recognizes that bands, bodyweight and home-based routines can be effective. It does not identify isometric holds as a complete standalone program [3]. That is a sensible frame: choose the form of resistance that suits your circumstances, and include the kinds of movement and effort that match your goals. If you want to improve strength through a moving range, practising only one fixed position leaves that part of the task untrained.

If you are new to holds, start with an exercise you can set up safely and perform without pain. A wall sit offers an accessible example, but it is not compulsory; a supported split-stance hold or a gentle press against a stable surface may suit you better. Use a clear space and make sure the surface will not slide or tip.

1. Choose a position you can enter and leave comfortably. For a wall sit, place your back against the wall and walk your feet forward until your knees are bent only as far as feels manageable. You do not need to reach a particular depth.
2. Hold for a brief, controlled interval—perhaps 10 to 20 seconds at first—while breathing normally. The goal is steady effort, not a contest to endure discomfort.
3. Stand or release with control, then rest until you feel ready to repeat. One or two additional holds is a modest starting point; reduce the time or stop if your position becomes difficult to control.
4. Record the exercise, position and duration. If it feels comfortable across sessions, change one variable at a time, such as adding a few seconds or choosing a slightly different position. You can also add a dynamic exercise rather than extending the hold indefinitely.

These are starting options, not a universal prescription. If you have a health condition, a recent injury or uncertainty about which positions are appropriate, ask a qualified health or exercise professional for guidance. Stop if you feel sharp pain, dizziness or unusual symptoms.
Measure the thing you actually trained

A hold can feel easier because you have learned to brace, balance or tolerate the position—not necessarily because every kind of strength has improved equally. That is still useful information: performance in the hold has changed. To track it clearly, keep the setup consistent. Note the position, the approximate joint angle or depth, the duration and how controlled the effort felt. Changing the position substantially between attempts makes comparisons harder to interpret.

Avoid treating duration as the only meaningful score. A longer hold may be one form of progress, but so might a more demanding position held for the same time, or completing a controlled movement that was previously difficult. Choose a measure tied to your reason for training. If your goal is a dynamic task, include that task in your practice and assess it directly rather than assuming a static-hold result will predict it.

Stillness can be a useful way to practise force, but it is not a substitute for asking what your training needs to prepare you to do. Isometrics make sense when the position itself matters, when they help you practise control, or when they are a convenient part of the session you can sustain. They are less convincing as a blanket replacement for resistance exercises that move through a range, because the evidence does not show that one training mode wins across every strength outcome.

A practical plan can include both: a brief hold in a relevant position, followed by controlled repetitions of a movement that uses that position. Keep the dose manageable and let your goal—not the novelty of an exercise—decide whether it belongs. The strength of staying put is real when it is measured honestly: a specific capacity, developed in a specific way, and used alongside the rest of a well-rounded approach.
